c1.story:
Walk into any chemist in Lucknow and ask for a diabetes tablet. The chemist reaches for the brand your doctor wrote down, you pay cash, and you will come back next month for the same strip, and the month after that, for years. Now picture a pharmacy in Ohio dispensing the very same molecule. Nobody there knows or cares which company made it. A wholesaler bought it at the lowest price it could find, and next year it will ask for a lower one.

Same chemistry, same Indian factory perhaps, two completely different businesses. That is the first thing to understand about Indian pharma, and it is why the word ‘pharma stock’ hides more than it reveals.

Behind the first door sit the domestic brand builders. Ramesh Juneja built Mankind by sending reps to the small-town doctors the big companies ignored; Torrent and Alkem built theirs in heart drugs and antibiotics respectively. Behind the second door sit the exporters who learned to copy American drugs the day their patents expire: Sun, Dr Reddy's, Lupin, Cipla. Behind the third sit the makers of the active ingredient itself, the chemistry shops that supply everyone else; Murali Divi turned Divi's into one of the world's most trusted of these. And behind the fourth sit the long-shot builders, Biocon under Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw or Zydus with its own discovered molecules, spending heavily today for approvals that may arrive years later.

In Indian pharma, the same pill can be a compounding annuity in Lucknow and a melting ice cube in Ohio.

Here's why the door matters so much. A headline about American drug tariffs knocks the second door and barely touches the first. A US law pushing drug makers away from Chinese suppliers is a gift to the third door. A patent settlement in a Delaware court can make or break a year for the fourth. One sector, four sets of news, four different reactions.

Most large companies straddle doors. Sun sells Indian brands, American generics and its own patented skin and eye drugs. Cipla sells respiratory brands at home and inhalers abroad. That is fine; it just means you value each piece separately, because the market reprices each piece at a different moment.
c1.read:
The four tiles above are the four doors. Read each one from top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it tell you how the product reaches the buyer: by brand and medical rep in India, by tender to three American buying groups, by bulk or contract supply to another drug maker, or not yet at all for the biosimilar and new-drug hopefuls.
  • The tickers are listed names that mostly sit behind that door. Click one to open its stock page. Notice AUROPHARMA under contract and API makers: it is also a large US generics seller, a straddler in the sense of the story.
  • The bar shows how much of the profit the company keeps rather than handing it to buyers or suppliers. Domestic brands sit at the high end, because the patient pays cash and the doctor prescribes by habit. US generics and API makers sit in the middle, squeezed by buyers but still earning a living. Biosimilar and new-drug hopefuls sit at the low end, not because the business is bad but because today's spending dwarfs today's sales; the bar measures the present, not the promise.
  • The last line is the bet you are making when you own a stock of that type.

The quickest test for any name: open its latest investor presentation and find the revenue split by geography. The share coming from India versus the US tells you, in one glance, which tile carries the stock.

c2.story:
Think of Indian pharma as a kitchen with five stations, and start at the back door, because that is where the uncomfortable truth lives.

Station one is the pantry: key starting materials and intermediates, the chemicals a few reaction steps away from the finished drug molecule. India, the self-styled pharmacy of the world, buys most of this pantry from China. Nobody worried much until January 2020, when Wuhan, a hub of that supply chain, went into lockdown. Prices of some ingredients jumped within weeks, and in March 2020 India restricted exports of a list of drug ingredients, paracetamol among them, to protect its own shelves. Delhi's answer was the production-linked incentive scheme for bulk drugs, which pays Indian companies to make these chemicals at home. It has brought back a few products, penicillin among them, but not the bulk of the pantry.

Station two is where the active ingredient, the molecule that actually treats the disease, gets made in large reactors. This is chemistry country: the industrial belts around Hyderabad and the coast near Visakhapatnam, home to Divi's, Laurus and Aurobindo's ingredient plants.

Station three is where the money is made or lost. The ingredient becomes a tablet, an injection, an inhaler, in a plant that must be blessed by regulators, the US Food and Drug Administration above all. An American inspector can arrive with little notice, walk the floors, read the batch records, and decide whether that plant can ship to the world's richest market.

Station four is distribution, and it splits in two. In India, a chain of stockists and chemists is fed by an army of medical representatives who visit doctors. In the US, three giant buying groups purchase almost all generic drugs and set the price.

Station five is who writes and who pays. In India, the doctor writes and the patient mostly pays out of pocket. In the US, an insurer or pharmacy benefit manager pays, and nobody at the counter cares whose name is on the bottle.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, then the two rows of bands underneath.

The boxes are the stations, from chemical pantry on the left to doctor and payer on the right. Stations two and three are highlighted: those are where India's listed names stand. Read the ‘who’ line in each box and watch the cast change, from Chinese chemical makers, to DIVISLAB and LAURUSLABS, to SUNPHARMA, CIPLA and DRREDDY, to stockists and American wholesalers, to doctors and insurers.

The first band row labels who holds each station. The left cell is coloured as the rival, China, because it owns the pantry. The two India listed cells sit in the middle. The two right cells belong to people the companies sell to, not people they control.

The second band row shows China's reach, drawn across the first four stations with the final cell marked World. Read it as reach, heaviest on the left: China dominates the pantry, competes at scale in active ingredients, and is a thinner presence further right, where Indian plants still supply a large share of America's generic pills.

Then use the map. A price spike in Chinese intermediates at station one reaches Indian gross margins within about a quarter. A warning letter at station three freezes launches. A buying group squeezing at station four is the yearly price erosion. Every pharma headline lands somewhere on this row; place it before you react to it.

c3.story:
Pharma's customers come in very different temperaments, and the temperament decides how predictable the earnings are.

The most valuable customer in the sector is a middle-aged Indian with diabetes, high blood pressure or a heart condition. He takes his tablets every day for the rest of his life, he trusts the brand his doctor chose, and he rarely asks the chemist for something cheaper. Lifestyle disease and an ageing population keep adding to his numbers every year. There is almost no cycle here, which is why chronic-heavy companies like Torrent trade at the multiples they do.

His cousin, the acute patient, is moodier. He buys antibiotics, painkillers, cough syrups and stomach remedies when he falls ill, which depends on the monsoon, the winter and whatever virus is going round. Alkem, the country's largest anti-infectives player, feels a mild flu season as a soft quarter. That is the calendar, not the business.

Then come the customers abroad. American wholesalers and pharmacies buy generic tablets and injectables at tender prices, and what moves them is the patent calendar, how many rivals got approved for the same molecule, and whether there is a shortage. Global drug makers buy active ingredients and contract manufacturing, and they are moving with China+1, the wish to have a non-Chinese supplier. Emerging markets in Africa, Russia and Latin America buy branded generics, where local currencies can wipe out a year's growth in rupee terms.

Closer to home, the government buys through lowest-price tenders and the Jan Aushadhi generic pharmacy chain, which is volume without much margin. And the over-the-counter consumer, buying condoms, pregnancy tests, vitamins and antacids, responds to advertising and to modern retail. Mankind's Manforce and Prega News show how far a pharma company can stretch into consumer branding.

The Indian chronic patient pays the dividend. The American pharmacy decides the surprise.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who is buying.
  • The second line is what they buy: chronic tablets, acute courses, tendered generics, active ingredients, branded generics abroad, scheme medicines, consumer products.
  • The third line is what moves that customer, and it is your watchlist outside the company.

A useful way to read the grid is to sort the tiles by rhythm. The chronic Indian patient has almost none, so it is the steady base. The acute patient follows the seasons, so a weak quarter there is usually the weather. The American wholesaler follows the patent calendar and the count of approved rivals. Global drug makers follow sourcing policy and their own pipelines. Emerging markets follow currencies. Government follows budgets and tenders.

Now count how many tiles a company sells into. A company with most of its sales in the first tile is a compounder; one with most in the third is a launch-and-erosion story; one with most in the fourth depends on a handful of customers. That maps straight back to the four doors on card one.

Finally, read the so-what line under the grid. It is the single sentence to remember: India is the coupon, the US is the option, and the quarter's surprise almost always comes from the American side.

c4.story:
Strip a pharma company to its essentials and you will find something odd. Unlike chemicals or steel, the raw material is not the main cost. The tablet itself is cheap to make. What costs money is everything around it: persuading doctors to prescribe it, proving to regulators that it is safe, and filing the paperwork to sell it in America.

In the domestic business, the biggest cost after materials is the field force. Thousands of medical representatives fan out every morning to clinics across the country, carrying samples and detailing aids, trying to stay in the doctor's mind. Productivity per rep is the whole game: a company whose sales grow faster than its rep count is compounding, and one hiring reps faster than sales grow is buying market share at a price.

In the export business, two other lines matter. Research and development spending, mostly on generic filings and the occasional trial, is a high single-digit share of sales for the big exporters. Cut it and this year's margin looks better while next year's launch calendar starves. And working capital is fat, because American customers pay slowly and inventory of several months is normal.

In domestic pharma the pill is cheap and the handshake is expensive.

Then come the lumpy lines. A new injectable or biologics block starts depreciating the day it opens, before it fills. Interest barely matters, because most large companies sit on net cash. But exceptional items can sting: patent litigation, settlements from the US price-fixing investigations that swept up several generic makers, and the cost of remediating a plant after a warning letter.

Finally, beware the flattering gross margin. When the generic of the blood-cancer drug lenalidomide was sold in limited volumes under patent settlements, it fattened the margins of several Indian exporters for years. A margin that rises on one big launch is borrowed from the year the launch ends.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, for a domestic branded company and a US generics exporter. Start at the left of each chart and move right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees of sales.
  • The input bar is raw materials: ingredients, intermediates and packaging. For the domestic brand it is under a third of sales; for the exporter, a little over a third. Notice how small this is compared with a chemicals or metals chart. The product is not where the money goes.
  • The opex bar is the big one: reps, marketing, research and plant running costs. For the domestic brand it takes roughly two-fifths, the largest bite on the chart. The exporter spends a little less here, but more of that goes on research and filings rather than reps.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is a sliver for the domestic brand and noticeably larger for the exporter, which carries more plant per rupee of sales.
  • The last bar is what is left: a little under a quarter for the domestic brand, a little under a fifth for the exporter. That gap is the pricing power of a trusted brand.

These are illustrative shapes, not a company's accounts; hover a bar for the amount.

Below, the list marks which lines matter. Gross margin, selling spend, research and working capital get a clear yes. Interest gets a no, which is unusual: most big names hold net cash. Watch the one-off charges line, marked sometimes, because settlements and remediation costs arrive in lumps.

c5.story:
The Indian half of pharma barely has a cycle. People take blood-pressure tablets in recessions too. The stocks, however, trade on the export half, and that half has a very real cycle of American pricing, patent expiries and plant inspections.

Rewind to the years before 2019. The big American buyers had merged into three giant groups, and they used their size to squeeze generic suppliers hard. Prices of generics fell by the mid-to-high teens a year. At the same time, the FDA was finding problems in Indian plants: Sun's Halol plant drew a warning letter in 2015, Dr Reddy's got one for three plants the same year, and Lupin's Goa and Pithampur plants followed in 2017. By 2019 the sector sat at a decade-low valuation, unloved and cheap.

Then Covid arrived. Volumes jumped, the rupee weakened, and the Wuhan shutdown reminded the world how much it depended on China. Washington asked India for hydroxychloroquine in April 2020. Delhi launched the bulk-drug incentives, and the pharma index doubled.

The hangover came in 2022: price erosion returned, freight and raw-material costs spiked, and the index went nowhere while the market climbed. Then the tide turned again. American drug shortages made buyers less aggressive, erosion fell to single digits, and the lenalidomide windfall arrived. By 2024 Indian pharma had its best year in a decade, with contract makers also riding Washington's push away from Chinese suppliers.

Where are we now? Past the peak. In 2025 the US president threatened drug tariffs and most-favoured-nation pricing; generics were spared, but the overhang capped valuations. In 2026 lenalidomide goes fully generic and the windfall ends, while the Indian patent on semaglutide, the blockbuster weight-loss and diabetes injectable, lapses and opens a price war at home. The next leg, biosimilars for cancer drugs from Zydus and Biocon among others, is visible but still a year or more away.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands. One caveat first, from the bold line above the story: this clock describes the export engine. The domestic half barely moves on it.

The clock has four arcs: boom at the top right, then peak, bust and bottom going clockwise. The years under each arc are the last full loop: boom in 2020 to 2021, peak in 2021, bust in 2022, bottom in 2023. The arrow is on the next loop. After the 2023 bottom came the 2024 boom, and the arrow now points low on the dial, around half past five, at the tail of the peak arc and heading into bust. The label reads past the export peak, in red. Hover an arc to see what defined that phase.

The timeline retells it year by year. Count the colours: bust in 2019, boom in 2020 to 2021, bust in 2022, a neutral turn in 2023, boom in 2024, neutral in 2025, and 2026 marked now.

The four hands let you move the arrow yourself.

  • US price erosion: mid single digits, flat. Kind for now; back above the low teens and exporter margins break.
  • Domestic growth versus volume: a diamond, price-led growth. Fine, but soft volumes eventually draw the regulator's eye.
  • FDA inspection outcomes: a diamond, mixed.
  • Chinese intermediate prices: soft, with an up arrow. The arrow marks the effect, not the price: soft input prices fatten Indian margins today.

c6.story:
A pharma exporter's results are shaped, to a surprising degree, by people who will never take its pills. A currency trader in Mumbai. A procurement head at an American buying group. A trade official in Washington. A price clerk at the pricing authority in Delhi.

Start with the rupee, because it is the cleanest mechanism on the board. An exporter bills American customers in dollars but pays most of its costs, scientists, plant workers, reps, in rupees. When the rupee weakens, every dollar of sales becomes more rupees while the cost base barely moves, so the extra drops almost straight to profit. That is why a sharp rupee fall lifts every exporter regardless of where the cycle stands.

Next, American price erosion, the yearly discount the three buying groups extract. It is set by how many competitors got approval for the same molecule and whether there is a shortage. When erosion runs in the mid-teens, an exporter needs a stream of new launches just to stand still. When it runs in single digits, the old portfolio holds its value and launches are pure growth.

The third heavy dial is new: American trade policy. In 2025 Washington announced national-security tariffs on imported branded drugs and pushed most-favoured-nation pricing, which would tie American prices to the lowest paid by other rich countries. Generics have been exempt so far. But even an exempt sector trades at a discount when the exemption could be withdrawn with a proclamation.

Then the quieter dials. Chinese intermediate prices squeeze gross margin for a quarter or two when they rise. Indian wholesale inflation sets the permitted yearly hike on price-controlled medicines each April. US rules against Chinese contract manufacturers send work to Indian makers. Health inflation and insurance support domestic pricing. Crude oil nudges solvent, packaging and freight costs. And when the broad market gets nervous, money rotates into pharma as a defensive hiding place.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: the route by which it reaches profits. This column tells you what to listen for on the next results call.
  • A rise does: a green up arrow means a rise helps, a red down arrow means it hurts, a diamond means it depends on the company.
  • Weight: one to three dots for how much it matters. Three dots can make or break a year.

Scan the three-dot rows first. There are three: the dollar against the rupee, US price erosion and US tariffs and pricing policy. Notice that the rupee is the only one of the three that helps when it rises; the other two both carry red arrows. That asymmetry is the export business in one glance: one friend you cannot control, two threats you cannot control either.

The two-dot rows are the second layer: Chinese intermediate prices hurting, Indian wholesale inflation and US rules against Chinese suppliers both helping.

The last column shows today's reading where a dial maps to a series we track: the rupee, Brent crude, the Indian money rate, the pharma index, and consumer inflation, both general and health. For the wholesale-inflation dial, read the general consumer price series as the nearest proxy we hold. The heaviest threats, erosion and tariffs, show a dash because no clean series exists; for those you rely on company commentary and Washington's announcements. The so-what line below names the two to track if you track nothing else: the rupee and erosion.

c7.story:
Every Indian pharma veteran knows the Ranbaxy story. In 2008 the FDA banned imports from two of its plants over data problems; years later the company pleaded guilty in America and paid a fine of half a billion dollars. Daiichi Sankyo, which had just bought it, ended up selling it to Sun. The lesson burned into the industry: in this business, the chemistry is rarely what fails. The paperwork, the culture and the honesty of the batch records are.

That is the first bottleneck, and it never quite goes away. One bad FDA inspection can block every new launch from a plant for two or three years. Most of the biggest names, Sun, Dr Reddy's, Lupin, Cipla, Aurobindo, have lived through it at least once. And the root cause is usually data integrity: missing records, retested samples, deleted files. Fixing that takes years, consultants and sometimes a change of management. The talent and quality-culture row exists for exactly this reason.

The second and third bottlenecks are structural. Roughly two-thirds of the chemical starting materials still come from China, so a Chinese shutdown or price spike lands straight on Indian margins. And three American buying groups purchase almost all US generics, so even a dozen Indian sellers chasing the same molecule have little pricing power.

Then come the domestic irritants. Essential medicines carry a ceiling price, and the pricing authority fines companies that overcharge. Every few years the health ministry bans fixed-dose combinations it deems irrational; Pfizer's Corex cough syrup was among the brands caught in the 2016 ban, which set off a long court fight. Trade generics, sold on chemist margin without promotion, and online pharmacies discounting in the cities slowly chip at the brand premium.

And finally, biologics: a biosimilar needs a decade and enormous capital before the first rupee of sales, and patent settlements decide the launch date. That is a barrier for newcomers and a moat for whoever gets through.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck with a reason and a severity label. The label tells you where the risk belongs in your thinking.

  • Structural: China for starting materials and the three US buyers. Permanent features that cap exporter returns. Price them into valuation, not into your news feed.
  • Recurring: FDA inspections, domestic price control and combination-drug bans. These come back again and again. Note that the FDA row is labelled recurring, not structural: it strikes one plant at a time and can be fixed, which is why a stock under a warning letter can be an opportunity once remediation is credible.
  • Slow: talent and quality culture, trade generics and online pharmacies. Gradual pressures that shift the landscape over years.
  • Two-sided: biologics capital and time. It keeps newcomers out and makes the survivors' biosimilars more valuable.

Read the table in the order the so-what suggests. The first three rows set the ceiling on how good the export business can ever be. The price-control and combination-ban rows are the headlines that knock a domestic stock for a day and rarely matter for a year; a ban usually hits a small slice of a big company's portfolio.

A practical habit: for each export name you own, keep a one-line note of every key plant's latest FDA status. That single list explains more surprises than any model.

c8.story:
Pharma is one of the most regulated businesses on earth, and in India it answers to two capitals at once: Delhi and Washington.

In Delhi, the drug regulator, CDSCO, approves new drugs and trials, licenses plants and bans irrational combinations. The pricing authority, NPPA, enforces the Drug Price Control Order: medicines on the national essential list carry a ceiling price, with a yearly hike linked to wholesale inflation. That covers roughly a sixth of the domestic market, so every expansion of the essential list pulls more brands under the cap. The Department of Pharmaceuticals runs the incentive schemes that pay companies to make starting materials at home.

Two newer Delhi rules deserve attention. After children died in Gambia and Uzbekistan in 2022 from Indian-made cough syrups, the government tightened Schedule M, its good-manufacturing rules; big companies had to comply in 2024 and small ones got until the end of 2025. Many small plants cannot afford the upgrade, which slowly consolidates the industry toward listed names. And the Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices of 2024 limits gifts and sponsored travel for doctors, changing how reps win prescriptions, though enforcement is patchy.

Indian patent law is a regulator of its own. It sets a high bar for evergreening, minor tweaks to extend a patent; Novartis lost its fight over the cancer drug Glivec in the Supreme Court in 2013 on exactly that point. Patent expiry dates set launch dates, and the semaglutide lapse in 2026 is the live example of a date-driven price war.

In Washington, the FDA inspects every plant that ships to America and approves each generic filing. A warning letter freezes approvals; an import alert blocks the plant entirely. And American trade policy, tariffs on branded drugs with generics exempt for now, has become the single biggest policy risk for exporters. A proposed law restricting Chinese biotech suppliers sits in the wings as a potential tailwind for Indian contract makers.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why you should care, and its status.

The status column is how to prioritise.

  • Always: CDSCO, the pricing authority, the US FDA and the Patents Act. Permanent fixtures. They rarely make headlines, but when they do, it is a same-day stock move: a combination ban, a price cap, a warning letter, a patent ruling.
  • Live: the Department of Pharmaceuticals and its incentives, US trade policy, revised Schedule M and the marketing code. These are shaping the industry right now. US trade policy is the one row to read twice, because its ‘why you care’ cell calls the generics exemption the biggest single policy risk.
  • Coming: the US law restricting Chinese biotech suppliers. A tailwind for contract makers if it passes in full; until then, treat it as optionality, not earnings.

Notice there is no ‘new’ row this time. Pharma's rules are mostly old rules applied harder, which is why the table leans on ‘always’ and ‘live’.

Also notice the split between Delhi and Washington. Delhi's rows mostly touch domestic brand owners; Washington's rows touch exporters. Match the rows to the doors on card one and you know which regulator to watch for each stock you own.

Dated regulatory news, filtered for this industry from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces boils down to a single question: once the money comes in, who gets to keep it? Run the two halves of Indian pharma through that test and you get two very different answers.

Start with the buyer, because that is where the gap is widest. The Indian patient pays cash, follows the doctor and rarely switches brands, so the buyer has little power. The American buyer is the opposite. Three buying groups purchase almost everything, run a reverse auction every year, and drop a supplier who will not match the lowest bid. Same molecule, opposite bargaining power.

Rivalry tells a similar story. At home, thousands of brands compete, but doctors prescribe by habit, so a well-known brand holds its share for years. In the US, when a blockbuster loses patent protection, a dozen generic makers, many of them Indian, can win approval for the same molecule. The price can collapse to a sliver of the branded price within months. The only shelter is being first: the first company to successfully challenge a patent wins a hundred and eighty days of near-exclusive sales, the richest window in generics.

New entrants? Anyone can file an American generic application, but building a trusted Indian brand and a national field force takes a decade. That is why the domestic franchises Mankind and Torrent built are so hard to copy.

Substitutes nibble at both. In India, trade generics and online discounts tempt the price-conscious. In the US, a new approval or an authorised generic, the brand owner's own cheap copy, can replace you within a quarter.

Suppliers, mainly Chinese intermediate makers, have some power over everyone, a little more over commodity generics than over branded chronic drugs.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force puts on the business. So a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: India branded formulations and US generics exporters. Look at the overall size first. The US generics shape is larger on every single spoke; there is no crossing point. That is unusual in these charts and it says something blunt: the export business is under more pressure from every direction at once.

Then find the spoke with the biggest gap. It is the buyer spoke: one for the Indian brand, three, the maximum, for the US exporter. Rivalry is next, two against three, then substitutes, one and a half against two and a half. Suppliers and entrants show smaller gaps.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero, no pressure, to three, heavy pressure, with a one-line reason. Read the reasons, not just the numbers; the buyer reason, cash-paying patients against three US buying groups, is the whole argument in a sentence.

What the chart does not draw is the contract maker. The so-what line places it: it keeps a good share as long as the customer stays, which is why a single lost contract hurts so much. If you own a company that straddles doors, mentally blend the two shapes in proportion to its revenue split.

c10.story:
A pharma results call can bury you in molecule names, filing counts and therapy-area growth rates. Most of it is noise. Eight numbers tell you almost everything, and you can read them in a few minutes.

Gross margin comes first, because it captures two forces in one number: American price erosion from the selling side and Chinese ingredient prices from the buying side. A sudden jump deserves a question: is it a durable mix shift toward brands and specialty, or one launch that will fade?

EBITDA margin comes next. It tells you whether the field force and the research budget are being paid for. Then domestic growth against the market. India's audited pharma market grows high single to low double digits a year, so a company growing a few points faster is taking prescriptions from rivals. Ask whether that growth comes from volume or merely from price hikes; price alone means the brand is ageing.

Then the three export numbers that rarely appear in a filing. What management says about US price erosion tells you where the pricing cycle stands. Research spending as a share of sales tells you whether the launch pipeline is being fed; a sudden drop flatters this year at the expense of the next. And the count of pending filings and expected launches, especially complex injectables or first-to-file products, is next year's US revenue in embryo.

Plant inspection status deserves its own line because it can override all the others. Every key plant should be classified acceptable, with no open warning letters. One red flag there freezes the launch list overnight.

Finally, return on capital tells you whether the whole mix of brands and plants earns more than it costs to fund. Domestic brand owners, light on capital, should clear a higher bar than exporters.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of each company you own.
  • What good looks like is the benchmark, and it is the only place on the page with figures. Notice that several rows give different marks for each door: branded formulations, exporters, API makers. Always compare a company with its own door's mark, not the highest one.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of this industry's listed companies in our database. Four rows carry one: gross margin, EBITDA margin, sales growth and return on capital. The other four show a dash, because US erosion commentary, research share, the filing pipeline and inspection status live in calls, presentations and FDA records rather than in standard filings. Those four you gather yourself.

A caution on the median: it pools every listed company with filings, large and small, across all four doors. Read it as a picture of the typical listed pharma company, not of the big names in the headlines.

The trick is to triangulate three things for any company: its own number, its door's good mark, and the median. A domestic brand owner well above both on margin and return on capital is the compounder the call favours.

c11.story:
The best early warnings about Indian pharma rarely come from Indian pharma companies. They come from databases and documents most investors never open.

The FDA publishes inspection classifications and warning letters; a plant flagged today shows up as missing US launches a couple of quarters later. The American drug shortage list is a pricing thermometer: when it lengthens, buyers stop squeezing the suppliers who can still ship. The monthly audits of Indian prescription sales reveal domestic growth and volume weeks before results. India's wholesale inflation print sets the permitted price hike on controlled medicines from April. Chinese ingredient prices reach Indian gross margins within a quarter. And the US patent and litigation calendar, the settlements and court dates for the big molecules, tells you two quarters or more ahead which launches are coming and which windfalls are ending.

Then there are the same-day movers. A tariff proclamation from the White House reprices exporters within hours, even when the exemption holds. And the rupee translates the quarter's export revenue at whatever rate it happens to be.

Put the signals together and you get a simple rule. The export half is in an up-cycle when US erosion is in single digits, the big plants are inspection-clean, and the launch calendar carries complex products. The domestic half needs only steady volumes and a permitted price hike.

Score it today and one of three is on. Erosion is kind, mid single digits and holding. But several large plants are under review, and the complex launches meant to replace the lenalidomide windfall, biosimilars above all, are still a year out. That is why the call leans toward domestic brands and contract makers and is selective on US generics: the cushion is fading before the replacement has arrived.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal along a line by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read the channel through which it reaches earnings.

  • Same quarter, far left: monthly Indian prescription data, US tariff proclamations and the dollar-rupee rate. These tell you what is already happening.
  • One quarter ahead: FDA inspection classifications, the US shortage list, the wholesale inflation print and Chinese ingredient prices. The busiest column on the chart, and the one to check every month.
  • Two quarters ahead, furthest right: the US patent expiry and litigation calendar. It is the earliest warning on the chart, because court dates and settlements fix launch quarters long in advance.

Use the chart as a reading order: start on the right, confirm in the middle, and treat the left as the scoreboard.

Below the chart sits the three-sign rule. A tick means the sign is on, a cross means it is not, and the note gives today's state. Today it reads one tick and two crosses: erosion in single digits is on; inspection-clean plants and complex launches replacing the windfall are off. The domestic half is not scored on these signs; its test is simpler, steady volume plus a permitted price hike.

Finally, the call box gives the view, the three points behind it and what would change it. Treat the would-change items as alerts: tariffs extended to generics, a wave of clean inspections at the big exporters, or a sharp rupee fall. If one appears, the call is due for a rethink.
